Title: $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is flexibly stable in the operator norm
Authors: Alexander Lubotzky, Guy Salomon
Date: Mon Jul 20 05:47:04 2026

A cornerstone of stability theory is Voiculescu's 1983 counterexample: he constructed a sequence of pairs of unitary matrices whose commutators converge to zero in the operator norm, but whose distances from the set of commuting unitary pairs remain bounded away from zero. Namely, the group $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is not stable in the operator norm. We prove, somewhat surprisingly, that stability is restored after an asymptotically negligible enlargement of the dimension. That is, the group $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is flexibly stable in the operator norm. This provides the first example, in any context, of a flexibly stable group that is not stable. Building on a construction of Eckhardt, who produced finitely generated amenable groups that are very-flexibly stable but not flexibly stable in the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt norm, we show that the same groups exhibit the analogous separation in the operator norm: they are very-flexibly stable but not flexibly stable.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 Almost commuting unitaries

The main topic of this paper is finite dimensional unitary representations, and approximate representations, of discrete groups. However, we will start with a more basic question about matrices as that motivates our main questions and results; informally, it asks if any pair of approximately commuting unitary matrices can be approximated by an actually commuting pair.

All norms in this paper are operator norms on spaces of bounded operators on (possibly finite dimensional) Hilbert spaces.

**Question 1.1.** *For any* ε > 0, *does there exist* δ > 0 *with the following property?*

*For any* n¹, *if* u, v ∈ Mₙ(C) *are unitary matrices satisfying*

‖uv − vu‖ < δ,

*then there are unitary matrices* u′, v′ ∈ Mₙ(C) *satisfying*

‖u′ − u‖ < ε, ‖v′ − v‖ < ε, *and* u′v′ = v′u′.

The question is completely answered by the following result. To state it, we need some notation. Let u, v ∈ Mₙ(C) be unitary matrices such that ‖uv − vu‖ < 1. The function

[0, 1] ∋ t ↦ det(t + (1 − t)uvu⁻¹v⁻¹)  (1)

then defines a path in the complex numbers that starts and ends at 1, and avoids 0. Hence we may define w(u, v) to be the winding number of this path.

**Theorem 1.2** (Several contributors - see below).  
(i) There is ε > 0 such that for any n, if u, v ∈ Mₙ(C) are unitary matrices such that ‖uv − vu‖ < 1 and w(u, v) ≠ 0, then there do not exist unitary matrices u′, v′ ∈ Mₙ(C) with ‖u′ − u‖ < ε, ‖v′ − v‖ < ε and u′v′ = v′u′.  
(ii) For any ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that for any n, if u, v ∈ Mₙ(C) are unitary matrices satisfying ‖uv − vu‖ < δ and w(u, v) = 0, then there are unitary matrices u′ and v′ satisfying ‖u′ − u‖ < ε, ‖v′ − v‖ < ε and u′v′ = v′u′.

Moreover, for any δ > 0 and k ∈ Z there exist n and unitary matrices u, v ∈ Mₙ(C) with ‖uv − vu‖ < δ and w(u, v) = k.

In brief, Theorem 1.2 says there is a robust integer-valued topological invariant w(u, v) that completely determines whether an almost solution of the equation “uv = vu” is close to an actual solution.

Part (i) has its roots in work of Voiculescu [134]. The interpretation in terms of winding numbers comes from work of Loring [99] and of Exel

¹The order of quantifiers is crucial: if δ is allowed to depend on n, the answer is different.

#### Subgroups with all finite lifts isomorphic are conjugate
Ido Karshon, Alexander Lubotzky, D. B. McReynolds, Alan W. Reid, Mark Shusterman

We show that for non-conjugate subgroups $G_1$ and $G_2$ of a finite group $G$ there exists an extension of $G$ (by a finite group) in which the pre-images of $G_1$ and $G_2$ are not isomorphic. This allows us to show that $\mathbb Z$-coset equivalent subgroups of a finite group are not necessarily isomorphic, answering a question of Dipendra Prasad. We also indicate connections to profinite rigidity, anabelian geometry, mapping class groups, and non-arithmetic lattices in Lie groups.

The paper proves that the group $\mathbb{Z}^2$Z 2 is flexibly stable in the operator norm, despite not being stable in that norm. This result provides the first known instance in mathematical literature where these two stability notions are strictly separated.

### Core Theoretical Framework

The authors define stability for a group $\Gamma$Γ with respect to a sequence of unitary groups $U_{d_n}$U d n​​ equipped with a normalized unitarily invariant matrix norm $\|\cdot\|_*$∥⋅∥∗​. A sequence of "challenges" (asymptotic representations) $\phi_n: \Gamma \to U_{d_n}$ϕ n​:Γ→U d n​​ satisfies $\|\phi_n(gh) - \phi_n(g)\phi_n(h)\|_* \to 0$∥ϕ n​(g h)−ϕ n​(g)ϕ n​(h)∥∗​→0.

  * Stability: Requires the existence of representations $\pi_n: \Gamma \to U_{d_n}$π n​:Γ→U d n​​ such that $\|\pi_n(g) - \phi_n(g)\|_* \to 0$∥π n​(g)−ϕ n​(g)∥∗​→0.
  * Flexible Stability: Requires representations $\pi_n: \Gamma \to U_{k_n}$π n​:Γ→U k n​​ and isometries $W_n: \mathbb{C}^{d_n} \to \mathbb{C}^{k_n}$W n​:C d n​→C k n​ such that $\frac{k_n}{d_n} \to 1$d n​k n​​→1 and $\|W_n^* \pi_n(g) W_n - \phi_n(g)\|_* \to 0$∥W n∗​π n​(g)W n​−ϕ n​(g)∥∗​→0.
  * Very-flexible Stability: Allows an arbitrary finite-dimensional enlargement ($k_n \ge d_n$k n​≥d n​ with no constraint on the ratio).

### Methodology for $\mathbb{Z}^2$Z 2

Voiculescu’s 1983 counterexample established that $\mathbb{Z}^2$Z 2 is not stable in the operator norm by constructing pairs of unitaries $(u_n, v_n)$(u n​,v n​) that almost commute but possess a non-vanishing winding number obstruction.   3. Application of Gong–Lin / Eilers–Loring–Pedersen: Relying on the theorem that almost-commuting unitaries with vanishing winding number can be approximated by commuting unitaries, the authors demonstrate that the augmented matrices $(X_n, Y_n)$(X n​,Y n​) can be approximated by commuting unitaries $(U_n, V_n)$(U n​,V n​) in $U_{k_n}$U k n​​.

### Separation of Stability Notions

The authors extend their analysis by building on Eckhardt's work to show that not all very-flexibly stable groups are flexibly stable. By considering finitely generated, residually finite, amenable groups where certain traces are not limits of finite-dimensional traces, they prove that there exist groups (such as specific subgroups of $GL_5(\mathbb{Z}[1/p])$G L 5​(Z[1/p])) that are very-flexibly stable but fail to be flexibly stable in the operator norm.
